# What's different between last week and this week?

## What's different between last week and this week?


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}

**Last week, we knew the population we wanted to compare our sample to:**

<br>

```{r echo=F, fig.width=5, fig.height=3, fig.align = 'center'}

mu <- 100
sigma <- 15

x <- seq((mu - 4*sigma), (mu + 4*sigma), length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y)

p_iq_pop <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#0F4C81") +
  labs(x = "IQ scores in the population", y = "Density") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(
    (mu - 4*sigma), (mu + 4*sigma), by = sigma)
    ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  NULL

p_iq_pop
```

:::
:::{.column width="10%"}
:::
:::{.column width="45%"}

**From now on, we do not know the population that we want to compare any of our samples to.**

<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

:::hcenter
**???**
:::

:::
::::


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="45%"}

- Our RQ asked whether bilingual adults had a higher IQ than the general population.
- We knew that in the population, IQ is normally distributed with mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15.
- This let us come up with the null distribution—what sample means **would** look like **if** H0 were true—based on properties of the population.

:::
:::{.column width="10%"}
:::
:::{.column width="45%"}

- Real life is basically always like this: we don't know the true population mean or how variable the population is.
- So we can't use the population to figure out our null distribution.
- **So how do we know what to compare our sample to?**

:::
::::


## The answer: The t-distribution

```{r echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.5}
#| out.width: 1000px

x <- seq(-6, 6, length.out = 1000)
y <- dt(x, df = 2)
z <- dnorm(x)
df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, z = z)

p_t <- ggplot(df, aes(x = x, y = y)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "seagreen4") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(
    x = x,
    ymin = 0,
    ymax = y
  ), 
  fill = 'seagreen4',
  alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "t", y = "Density") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  NULL

p_t
```

It looks a lot like a normal distribution (overlaid in blue), but it's less pointy in the middle and fatter at the tails.

```{r echo=F, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.5}
#| out.width: 1000px
p_t +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(x = x, ymin = 0, ymax = z),
    alpha = 0.4,
    fill = dapr1blue
  ) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', y = 0.3, x = 4, label = 'normal distribution\nwith mean 0, SD 1',
           colour = dapr1blue,
           family = 'Source Sans 3',
           size = 8) +
   geom_curve(x=1.5, xend=0.2, y=0.37, yend=0.38, col=dapr1blue, curvature = 0.2, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "npc")), linewidth = 1.5) +
  xlab(NULL) +
  NULL
```

The fat tails put more probability on extreme values, so that we don't rule them out as much, since after all we don't know what the population might look like.

## The t-distribution has different shapes

All of these are t-distributions with different **degrees of freedom (df):**

```{r echo=F, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5}
tibble(x = c(-5, 5)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 2), colour = '#85DB8F', linewidth = 2) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 5), colour = '#5DB367', linewidth = 2) +
  stat_function(fun = dt, args = list(df = 99), colour = '#528B59', linewidth = 2) +
  labs(x = 't', y = 'Density') +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.38, label = 'df = 2 ', colour = '#85DB8F', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.35, label = 'df = 5 ', colour = '#5DB367', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  annotate(geom = 'text', x = 3, y = 0.32, label = 'df = 99', colour = '#528B59', size = 9, family = 'Source Sans 3', hjust = 0) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  NULL
```

You don't need to know exactly what df is.
Just know that **it's closely related related to sample size:**

- if we have a sample size $n$ of 100, 
- then we have 99 degrees of freedom.
- **For tests involving t-distributions, the df is always $n - 1$.**

So our sample size determines the shape of the t-distribution that we will use as our null distribution.

Why does it work this way?
Because the more data we have, the better a guess we can make about the population.


# Let's do a t-test

## Let's do a t-test

<br>

Recall from last week the five steps of NHST:

1. Based on your RQ, define the null and alternative hypotheses.
2. Collect sample data and determine the appropriate null distribution.
3. Calculate the test statistic for our observed sample.
4. Make a decision about whether or not to reject H0.
5. Interpret this decision in the context of the RQ.

<br>

We'll go through them one by one as we walk through the logic of a **one-sample t-test.**


# Step 1: Based on RQ, define H0 and H1

## Our RQ this week

<br>

**RQ: In healthy adults, is average body temperature different from the standard reference value of 37C?**

<br>

**The null hypothesis (H0)** is always that any difference or effect we're interested in **does not exist.**

- So our H0 here is that average body temperature $\mu$ is equal to 37C.


::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In fancy math notation:

$$
H_0 : \mu = 37
$$
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In plain text:

:::{style="font-size:180%;"}
```
H0: mu = 37
```
:::

:::
::::


**The alternative hypothesis (H1)** is that the difference or effect we're interested in **does exist.**

- So our H1 here is that average body temperature is *not* equal to 37C.



::::{.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In fancy math notation:

$$
H_1 : \mu \neq 37
$$
:::
:::{.column width="50%"}
- In plain text:

:::{style="font-size:180%;"}
```
H0: mu != 37
```
:::

:::
::::

**Our key question: is this sample close to what we'd expect to see if H0 were true?**


## What would we expect to see if H0 were true?

A one-sample t-test measures the *difference* between our observed sample mean and some specific value stated in the RQ (here, it's 37C).

If H0 is true—if body temperatures in reality do have a mean of 37C—then the difference between our sample mean and the value 37 should be pretty small, close to zero:

[plot with vline at zero]


We should expect some variability too, because people are a bit different from one another and also sampling is random.
How much variability around zero should we expect, if the H0 is true?
That's exactly what the t-distribution tells us:

[same plot with t-distrib with df 49 I think TODO overlaid]


(The difference is measured not in degrees Celsius but in t-units.)

## Distributions from warm-up Wooclap (1)

Uncollapse code for the basic standard normal distribution plot.

```{r fig.width=7, fig.align='center', fig.height = 4}
#| code-fold: true
dapr1blue <- '#0F4C81'

m <- 0
sd <- 1
nx <- seq(m-4*sd, m+4*sd, length.out = 1000)

p_stdnorm <- tibble(
  x = nx,
  n_dens = dnorm(nx, m = m, sd = sd)
) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x, y = n_dens)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5, colour = dapr1blue) +
  labs(
    y = 'Density',
    x = 'Standard normal distribution'
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    text = element_text(family = 'Source Sans 3', size = 24),
    axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(color = dapr1blue)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(
    (m - 4*sd), (m + 4*sd), by = sd)
    ) +
  NULL
```

Uncollapse code for the following plot with the z-statistic and shaded area.

```{r fig.width=8, fig.align='center', fig.height = 4, warning = F}
#| code-fold: true
z <- 1.2
p_stdnorm +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      x = ifelse(x >= z, x, NA),
      ymin = 0,  ymax = n_dens),
    alpha = 0.3, fill = dapr1blue
    ) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = z, colour = 'tomato1', linewidth = 2) +
  NULL
```
